newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serb nationalists win bitter victory in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Serb nationalists win bitter victory in Bosnia.

text.p: From the day that the international community endorses their victory at Saturday's elections nothing will be the same for the hardline Bosnian Serb leaders, Western diplomats believe.
The world that day will give them the international legitimacy which they crave but will demand in return that they respect the Bosnian peace agreement which they hate.
Although opposition candidates made a credible showing in the Bosnian Serb republic, the hardliners' demands for separatism and intransigence have gained big majorities.
So why are some opposition leaders rubbing their hands with glee?
"Let them stew. They caused this mess, let them clear it themselves. I can only imagine their cries of "treason' if we were in power," one opposition candidate told Reuters on condition of anonymity.

He was referring to the pressure the world will put on the hardliners of the ruling SDS party for the extradition of war criminals, for cooperation with the inter-ethnic government and the opening of borders to allow thousands of refugees home.
Diplomats have warned the Bosnian Serbs they must behave according to international standards once their mini-state is recognised as part of unified Bosnia, or face severe consequences.

Bosnian Serbs have been warned that they will eventually have to give up their former leader Radovan Karadzic and his army commander General Ratko Mladic, both honoured by Serbs but indicted by the Hague War Crimes Tribunal.
"Whoever extradites them will be cursed for the next nine generations. He or she would not be safe anywhere the Serbs live in the world," Predrag Radic, the mayor of Banja Luka, told Reuters.

His opponent in presidential elections, Biljana Plavsic, Karadzic's loyal hardline replacement, is set to win and will be saddled with the issue. She has said she would not extradite either of the men.
She has also called the idea of reunifying Bosnia "monstrous", but that is exactly what she will have to do -- to dismantle borders and allow thousands of refugees back home.
SDS leaders shudder at the thought. "Some say even that Serb refugees wanting to go back to their homes in Moslem-controlled territory are traitors," Radic said.
The thousands of refugees, whose bitterness was so deftly exploited by nationalists before the elections, are a time bomb which could break the SDS and help reunify Bosnia.
"They want to go home, and the majority hates living where they are. Many of them are not industrial workers, and refuge in towns means dependence on almost non-existant welfare," Radic said
"So either the authorities let them go across and accept other ethnic groups, or face dissent, bitterness and trouble.
Diplomats said they were aware the Serb leaders would try to prevaricate as long as they could. "But we have instruments, very powerful and very effective, to make them comply," one said.
Radic said the West would probably need to use only economic means and corroborated this with sombre figures.
"The destruction goes into billions of dollars. Our production plants are working at only eight percent of capacity."
"We have 450,000 refugees including 18,000 parentless children, 160,000 engineers, 35,000 invalids, 240,000 unemployed people, and empty state coffers.
"Just to feed them at a subsistence level we need 360 million German marks -- an enormous sum when you compare it to our gross national product of 420 million marks."
Radic said the Serb leaders were conducting "a horrible foreign policy" that led to the alienation even of their former mentor, Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.
"It looks like they did their best to turn even our former friends into enemies. So how do you attract foreign capital?" he asked.

"Only by toeing the line and sticking to what they already agreed to in Dayton," the diplomat said. "That will be very hard for them but we expect them quietly to go along with us while protesting in public to smooth their supporters."
